articles.title: Why I Built Syndicator: Automating Blog Distribution Across X, Bluesky, Mastodon, Threads, and Nostr on a $0 Cloudflare Worker
articles.excerpt: After moving my blog to EmDash CMS, getting an article live finally felt frictionless. I finish a draft, push it over MCP from my terminal, and it is live at the edge in a second. And then comes the p…
articles.body: After moving my blog to EmDash CMS , getting an article live finally felt frictionless. I finish a draft, push it over MCP from my terminal, and it is live at the edge in a second. And then comes the part I hate: distribution . If you write technical posts and don't share them, nobody knows they exist. So right after finishing an article, instead of moving on to my next project, I was stuck doing 20 minutes of mind-numbing tab-switching—opening X, Bluesky, Mastodon, Threads, and a Nostr client, trimming the excerpt to fit five different character limits, and manually chaining self-replies. I looked at existing SaaS social schedulers, and none of them made sense for a developer blog. Paying $15 to $30 a month just to poll an RSS feed is absurd.

articles.title: Why your voice agent says "asterisk asterisk"
articles.excerpt: You build a voice agent. The LLM is sharp, the TTS voice is warm, the latency is And it says: "asterisk asterisk invoice hash forty two asterisk asterisk colon dollar one What the LLM actually returne…
articles.body: You build a voice agent. The LLM is sharp, the TTS voice is warm, the latency is good. You put it on a real phone number and call it. And it says: "asterisk asterisk invoice hash forty two asterisk asterisk colon dollar one comma two three four point five six due two zero two six dash one one dash one one" What the LLM actually returned was perfectly reasonable: **Invoice #42**: $1,234.56 due 2026-11-11. The LLM did nothing wrong. The TTS engine did nothing wrong. The bug is in the gap between them, and almost nobody budgets for it. Why this happens LLMs are trained overwhelmingly on written English — documentation, Markdown, code, articles. So they emit written English: **bold** , $1,234.56 , Dr. , 2026-11-11 , bullet lists, emoji. TTS engines expect prose.

articles.title: I got tired of waiting for APIs to be ready, so I built a mock server that runs on my laptop
articles.excerpt: Every project I work on hits the same wall: the front end is ready, but the API it calls isn't. Or it is, but it's slow, shared with five other teams, or it only fails in production. So I'd write a qu…
articles.body: Every project I work on hits the same wall: the front end is ready, but the API it calls isn't. Or it is, but it's slow, shared with five other teams, or it only fails in production. So I'd write a quick fake server, throw it away, and write another one next month. At some point I stopped and built the thing I kept rebuilding. It's called Zyvra , and it's a mock API server that runs on your own computer. What it does You create a mock service (it listens on its own local port), add an endpoint like GET /products , and give it a response. Your app points at it instead of the real API. That part is easy and every tool does it. The parts I wanted were these: Rules. The answer can depend on the request: path, query, headers or body.

articles.title: FreeBSD Capsicum requires a file-descriptor rights design
articles.excerpt: FreeBSD Capsicum requires a file-descriptor rights design Capsicum changes the security model for a FreeBSD process by moving authority into delegated descriptors. After cap_enter(2), the process cann…
articles.body: FreeBSD Capsicum requires a file-descriptor rights design Capsicum changes the security model for a FreeBSD process by moving authority into delegated descriptors. After cap_enter(2) , the process cannot freely reach global namespaces such as the filesystem or process table. It can operate through file descriptors and other capabilities it already holds. That model is useful for parsers and network services, but the boundary is only as good as the rights attached to every inherited descriptor. A common mistake is to treat capability mode as a filesystem chroot. The process may still use an already open directory, socket, pipe, or shared-memory object. Those handles can carry broad authority.

articles.body: In 1964, Italian director Sergio Leone redefined the Western movie genre with A Fistful of Dollars . Eschewing the relatively simplistic morality tales of earlier films, Leone’s protagonist wasn’t a noble hero, but an opportunistic gunslinger who pits two rival Old West gangs against each other to score a big payday. Despite the moral complexity of it all — or, more likely, because of it — A Fistful of Dollars was an international success that proved three things: audiences were ready for a new kind of Western, America no longer had a monopoly on the genre, and Clint Eastwood was a bankable movie star.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. articles.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
articles.excerpt: NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.
articles.body: A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.
articles.body: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space.

articles.body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR OpenAI has announced that it will retire ChatGPT Advanced and Standard voice on December 11, 2026. The company is focusing on unifying the voice experience through GPT-Live. Live video and screen sharing will continue to use Advanced voice until GPT-Live has this capability. Earlier this year, OpenAI rolled out a new voice model called GPT-Live . The Gemini Live rival joined ChatGPT Advanced and Standard voice as yet another way to have more natural conversations with the chatbot. As the saying goes, three is a crowd, and OpenAI is ready to do some streamlining. OpenAI has announced that a big change is coming for ChatGPT Voice.
